newsitem.title: USA: Mercedes Jan-April car sales, revenues up.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes Jan-April car sales, revenues up.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG's Mercedes passenger car division increased its worldwide revenues for the first four months of 1997 by 12.6 percent over a year ago, to about $11 billion, or 16.5 billion marks, Daimler management board member Juergen Hubbert said Thursday.

Hubbert, speaking to reporters at Mercedes-Benz' first U.S. assembly plant here, also said the division's profit for the period, to be detailed next week at the Daimler-Benz annual shareholders meeting, is expected to exceed the year-ago results.

Hubbert, who is in charge of Daimler-Benz' passenger vehicle operations, said Mercedes car sales for the January-April period rose 7.6 percent over year-ago record numbers to a total of 219,000 units.
Unit sales sales in Western Europe increased by more than four percent, sales in Japan rose by more than 20 percent, the United States increased by more than 25 percent during the period, he said.

But Mercedes' revenue growth exceeded volume growth because of an improvement in the car sales mix. "We achieved this by selling more expensive cars, such as the E-Class and the new SLK," he said in an interview.

Hubbert, who participated in grand opening ceremonies Wednesday, along with Daimler-Benz chairman Juergen Schrempp, and other top executives, said demand for Mercedes' new M-Class sport utility vehicle built here is expected to exceed supply.
Mercedes currently plans to build 65,000 of the vehicles annually at the facility near Tuscaloosa, Ala.

Hubbert estimated that the U.S. sport utility vehicle market will increase to 2.5 million units annually shortly after the turn of the century from about two million sold in 1996. "The volume in the top premium segment will even double" during that time, he said.
The M-Class is aimed just below the top end of the U.S. sport utility market, with an expected starting price of about $35,000.
He also reiterated that Daimler-Benz hopes to increase its Mercedes passenger vehicle volume to about one million units at the end of the decade from about 650,000 in 1996.
Mercedes' traditional models, the C, E, and S-Class cars, will account for about 700,000 units, while the remainder will be made up by new models, such as the A-Class, M-Class, SLK and CLK.
He said Mercedes hopes to raise its share of the worldwide passenger vehicle market to two percent during the same time frame from 1.6 percent currently.
